props.title: Alice in Wonderland
props.initialSlug: Prepare to fall down the rabbit hole.

sections.content: Tim Burton's Alice in Wonderland (2010) reimagines Lewis Carroll's classic through a darker, more mature lens. The film follows Burton's signature Gothic aesthetic, much like his work in Edward Scissorhands (1990) and Corpse Bride (2005). Mia Wasikowska's 19-year-old Alice returns to Wonderland (here called "Underland") in a story that borrows elements from both "Alice's Adventures in Wonderland" and "Through the Looking Glass." Johnny Depp's manic Mad Hatter and Helena Bonham Carter's Red Queen showcase Burton's penchant for eccentric characters, while the CGI-heavy visuals marked a departure from his earlier stop-motion style seen in The Nightmare Before Christmas (1993).

sections.content: The film sparked a trend of dark, live-action reimaginings of classic fairy tales, directly influencing Snow White and the Huntsman (2012), Maleficent (2014), and Cinderella (2015). Burton's version emphasizes female empowerment, transforming Alice from a curious child into a sword-wielding warrior who challenges Victorian-era gender expectations. This feminist revision aligns with other contemporary adaptations like Brave (2012) and Frozen (2013), which subvert traditional princess narratives. SUBHEAD: Visual Effects and Fantasy Filmmaking

The film's Oscar-winning Art Direction and Costume Design established a new standard for fantasy world-building, influencing later works like Oz the Great and Powerful (2013) and Beauty and the Beast (2017). The extensive use of CGI and green screen technology, while controversial among Burton purists, paved the way for modern fantasy blockbusters. This technical approach contrasts with the practical effects mastery of earlier fantasy films like The NeverEnding Story (1984) and Labyrinth (1986), marking a significant shift in how magical worlds are brought to screen.
